new.title: Detection of GRB 261010A with GRID-11B
new.summary: We report GRID-11B observations of the main emission episode of GRB 261010A. We measure $T_{90}=5.68^{+1.04}_{-0.32}$ s and a minimum variability timescale of $51.6^{+10.5}_{-9.8}$ ms. Its spectrum is described by a cutoff power law with $E_{\rm p}=1089^{+171}_{-80}$ keV. At both candidate host redshifts ($z=0.070$ and $0.785$), the low $\varepsilon$ values and their positions relative to the Amati relation suggest Type-I-like properties. These properties, despite the long duration, resemble those of GRB 211211A and motivate investigation of a possible compact-object merger origin.

new.title: Lost in the Signal Model: Confusion Between Deterministic and Stochastic Gravitational Wave Signals in Pulsar Timing Array Data
new.summary: With growing evidence for the presence of a gravitational wave background (GWB) in pulsar timing array (PTA) data, it is imperative to understand how this signal will act as a foreground for other GW signals, particularly those from individual supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs), which are predicted to be detected in the next decade. For PTAs, since these two types of signals are long-timescale persistent signals, a signal from an SMBHB system may already be present in the latest PTA datasets. In this work, we analyze how the presence of this signal could affect our detection statistics for the GWB, and how the presence of the GWB can affect our search for the SMBHB system. We find that individual SMBHB signals can significantly skew the recovery of the GWB amplitude and spectral index. However, when the SMBHB signals are recovered consistently, we are again able to recover the GWB power-law parameters, highlighting the importance of joint searches in future PTA searches for GWs. We also explore the rate of improvement of parameter estimation uncertainty, giving insight to the types of signals most likely to be identified well enough to enable multimessenger analyses.

new.title: Blazars through the eyes of REDSoX and GOSoX
new.summary: Blazar polarimetric properties provide key constraints on the physical conditions within relativistic jets, offering insights into particle acceleration mechanisms, high-energy radiation processes, and jet composition. The Rocket Experiment Demonstration of a Soft X-ray Polarimeter (REDSoX) will serve as a precursor to the Globe Orbiting Soft X-ray Polarimeter (GOSoX), a state-of-the-art polarimeter designed for observations in the soft X-ray range (0.2-0.4 keV), with a planned launch for 2030. REDSoX and GOSoX will be the first (and currently only) X-ray polarimeters capable of performing observations below 1 keV, opening a new observational window into high-energy polarimetry. In this work, we investigate the soft X-ray polarimetric properties of blazars expected in the REDSoX and GOSoX band and assess the detectability of different samples of sources: one drawn from the RoboPol Monitoring Program, a statistically complete sample of gamma-ray-selected blazars spanning the low-, intermediate-, and high-synchrotron-peaked sources, and one cross-matched between the CAZ (CRTS, ATLAS, and ZTF) and eROSITA catalogs. We estimated the expected source fluxes in the selected energy bands through spectral energy distribution fitting performed with the Bjet-MCMC tool. We investigated the expected polarimetric properties under three competing emission scenarios: leptonic, hadronic, and hybrid, each one predicting distinct observational signatures. We assessed the detectability of every source by comparing our polarization degree predictions with the instrument's minimum detectable polarization function (MDP). Finally, we computed the detection probability for each source. This work offers a set of promising blazar targets for future observations with GOSoX, highlighting the mission's potential for probing relativistic jet physics through soft X-ray polarimetry.

new.title: From Binary Wind to Radio Burst: Dispersion-Measure Evolution after Accretion-induced Collapse
new.summary: Secular changes in the dispersion measures (DMs) of repeating fast radio bursts probe the source-local plasma. Such DM time variability has been interpreted with spherical, single-density-profile models. Accretion-induced collapse (AIC) of a white dwarf may instead follow binary interaction and occur inside a finite, anisotropic circumstellar structure. Here, we construct an angle-dependent toy model of aspherical AIC ejecta propagating through a pre-AIC free wind, shocked-wind bubble, swept-up external shell, and polar cavity, exploring a diffuse environment (number density of $1~{\rm cm^{-3}}$, located at $10~$pc) and a compact cloud (number density of $500~{\rm cm^{-3}}$, located at $0.3~$pc), bracketing ionized and initially neutral upstream gas. The unshocked ejecta initially yield ${\rm DM}\propto t^{-2}$, while crossings of the finite wind-bubble interfaces produce breaks and curvature in ${\rm DM}(t)$. In initially neutral models, shock ionization can overcome geometric dilution: the total DM reverses from decline to growth after approximately $10$--$20$ yr and later turns over as the finite reservoir is processed. Ionized-upstream models instead generally decline or flatten. Without fitting individual sources, our models span both signs and the approximate magnitudes of the secular DM-variation rates measured among repeaters. In this dynamical framework, DM evolution is set by shock propagation through the circumsource density and ionization structure, rather than the contemporaneous burst rate, distinguishing it from photoionization-driven scenarios. Consequently, in our model, an instantaneous \(d{\rm DM}/dt\) is not a unique indicator of source age. We suggest that the observed distribution of secular DM variation slope amplitudes and signs will be important for distinguishing among different models of DM variations in repeating FRBs.

new.title: NGC 1300: A rich reservoir of ultraluminous X-ray sources
new.summary: We present the first systematic multi-epoch study of the X-ray source population of the barred spiral galaxy NGC 1300, using 12 archival Chandra observations spanning more than 15 years and archival Swift/XRT monitoring. Within the optical extent of the galaxy, we identify 42 X-ray sources, including six ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) and 13 ULX candidates. The candidates have measured luminosities below $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$, but their upper uncertainty bounds reach or exceed this threshold in at least one epoch. We examine source luminosities, long-term variability, broad-band spectral properties, and epoch-resolved X-ray luminosity functions (XLFs). Ten sources meet our transient criterion, seven have a variability significance of $S_{\rm var}\geq3$, and four meet both criteria. X32 is a highly variable ULX with a peak X-ray luminosity of $1.5\times10^{40}$ erg s$^{-1}$, more than 715 times the non-detection upper limit. The hardness-intensity diagrams show diverse spectral behavior among the luminous sources, with no common hardness-luminosity evolution. X32 remains predominantly hard despite its large luminosity variations, and its X-ray colors are consistent with the empirical high-mass X-ray binary (HMXB) region of the color-color diagram. The cumulative XLFs above $10^{38}$ erg s$^{-1}$ have slopes of $\beta\simeq0.6$ to $1.0$, with evidence for a broken power law in only a few epochs. The number of off-nuclear sources reaching $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$ ranges from zero to four per epoch. Long-term source variability thus strongly shapes the bright end of the XLF and makes the observed ULX census of NGC 1300 strongly epoch dependent. Multi-epoch monitoring is essential for establishing representative ULX populations in nearby galaxies.

new.title: Determining the Spin and Orbital Period of the Asynchronous Cataclysmic Variable X10 in 47 Tucanae
new.summary: The X-ray source X10 in the globular cluster 47 Tuc has been identified as a cataclysmic variable (CV). With a suggested 4.7 hour periodicity, and a soft X-ray spectrum, it appears to be an unusually X-ray luminous ($L_X=2.2\times10^{32}$ erg s$^{-1}$) polar CV. We use 286 ks of Chandra X-ray Observatory observations of 47 Tuc to study the X-ray timing behavior of 47 Tuc X10. X10 shows clear pulsations in the data, with occasional phase shifts. These suggest that X10 is an asynchronous polar CV, where the spin and orbital periods are slightly misaligned, and the dominant accretion flow shifts from one pole to the other. We use a Lomb-Scargle periodogram to suggest potential spin and orbital periods, then model the X-ray lightcurve using simple sinusoids to represent emission from each accretion pole, switching which pole is visible on the beat period. We find a white dwarf spin period of $P_{\mathrm{spin}} = 4.2683$ h and derive an orbital period of $P_{\mathrm{orb}} = 4.6779$ h from the beat modulation. This large degree of asynchronism (8.8%) suggests that X10 is in an unstable equilibrium, and may be a transitional system between an intermediate polar and a fully synchronized polar.

new.title: Disentangling Disk and Broad-Line Region Continuum Emission in a Sample of Active Galactic Nuclei
new.summary: Recent continuum reverberation-mapping measurements of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) indicate that the inter-band time lags are significantly larger than those predicted by the light travel times across the standard thin model. In addition, the observed $u$-band excess suggests the presence of diffuse continuum (DC) radiation originating in the broad-line region (BLR). Spectroscopically, the Balmer and Paschen jumps in DC emission are unique indicators to quantify the contributions of the BLR to the observed continuum. Here, we study the DC contributions of 31 AGNs, whose spectra are obtained with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) on the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and with X-shooter on the Very Large Telescope (VLT). In each spectrum, at least one of the Balmer and Paschen jumps is covered. For each object, we performed radiative transfer calculations using Cloudy within the Locally Optimally-emitting Clouds (LOC) model to construct source-specific DC spectral templates. We quantified the DC contribution by incorporating these templates as continuum components in spectral decomposition. The average ratio of the DC to total (i.e., disk+DC) continua is ~33% just below the Balmer jump (~3625 Å). The Balmer jump provides a stronger constraint on the DC component than the Paschen jump. Simulations based on mock spectra further demonstrate that an unsuitable template can introduce systematic, wavelength-dependent biases to the inferred DC fraction. Our results underscore the importance of employing appropriate DC templates in the spectral decomposition to infer the substantial DC contribution. Upcoming time-resolved spectra will enable more detailed modelling and tighter constraints on the disk and BLR.

new.title: Hard X-ray spectroscopy of a short-period asynchronous polar: IGR J19552+0044
new.summary: IGR J19552+0044 is an asynchronous polar with a beat modulation of $\approx2$ days due to $\approx3$% spin-orbit asynchronism. We present the first hard X-ray properties of this system using a NuSTAR observation. Spectral modeling yields a shock temperature of $kT_{\rm s}=44.50^{+3.60}_{-3.29}$ keV, implying a white dwarf mass of $M_{\rm WD}\geq 0.85\,M_\odot$. We infer an average accretion rate of $\dot{M}\sim 3.0\times 10^{-11}\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, consistent with expectations for short-period systems (orbital period $<2$ h). Even at this low accretion rate, we detect a significant Compton reflection component that gives a shock height of $H\sim 0.3\,R_{\rm WD}$. Time-resolved spectroscopy of the observation, covering $\approx61$% of a beat cycle, reveals a variation in $\dot{M}$ by a factor of $\sim 4.5$, providing X-ray evidence for the magnetic valve mechanism. Despite the large variations in $\dot{M}$, no significant change in shock temperature is observed. This weak thermal response constrains the shock structure on the white dwarf surface, favoring a shock height that remains approximately constant as $\dot{M}$ changes, potentially due to variations in the fractional accretion area $f$.

new.title: Modelling scintillation in Fast Radio Bursts
new.summary:
Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are bright, ms-duration, extragalactic radio transients. Propagation through inhomogeneities in the ionised medium produces scintillation, observed as frequency-dependent intensity variations in their spectra, with bright patches, called scintles. The characteristic scintillation bandwidth probes scattering material along the line of sight. Measuring this scale can be challenging when the observing bandwidth of the burst spectra contains a few scintles. We study the uncertainties associated with recovering $
u_s$ from frequency autocorrelation functions (ACFs) under finite-bandwidth conditions. We examine the recovery of $
u_s$ from individual ACFs and investigate if averaging multiple independent ACFs provides a more robust measurement. Using simulations, we reproduce observational conditions to investigate the modelling of scintillation in ACFs and the associated measurement uncertainties. We use these simulations to test the finite scintle error (FSE) prescription and assess its applicability to real observations. We test the resulting modelling framework on Effelsberg Ultra Broad Band receiver observations of the repeating FRB 20240114A. As the number of scintles decreases, individual ACFs develop fluctuations that deviate from the expected Lorentzian profile. This results in increased scatter in the recovered $
u_s$ and a less reliable FSE prescription. Averaging multiple independent ACFs mitigates these effects and improves the recovery of $
u_s$ in the low-scintle regime. Our results provide a framework for ACF modelling and uncertainty estimation in FRBs. For individual bursts, the FSE is effective with sufficient scintles; we find $\eta = 0.055$ more suitable for FRB analysis and update the FSE accordingly. For repeaters, averaging multiple ACFs and bootstrap resampling improve the recovery and uncertainty estimation of $
u_s$.

new.title: Probing for relativistic outflows in the Ultraluminous X-ray pulsar RX J0209.6-7427
new.summary: Context. Relativistic winds have been observed in Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs), but their detection at large distances remains limited. Galactic neutron stars accreting matter from Be-star companions provide a valuable opportunity to improve our understanding of these outflows. Aims. RX J0209.6-7427 is a Be-XRB, powered by a neutron star with a spin period of 9.3 seconds, that underwent an outburst in 2019, exceeding a bolometric luminosity of $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$ at its peak. Owing to its relatively low distance and a high-resolution XMM-Newton observation, this source is a strong candidate for investigating outflows associated with super-Eddington accretion. Methods. The RGS spectrum yields 105,000 counts, a factor of two higher than any other deep ULX RGS spectrum. RGS and EPIC-pn data sets were modelled with a phenomenological continuum accounting for emission from the accretion disc and accretion column. The emission and absorption features were fitted with the optically-thin plasma models available in SPEX, exploring the temperature-velocity parameter space. Results. The modelling of emission features suggests the presence of a multiphase photoionised plasma approximately at rest with respect to the source. The absorption features can be reproduced either by blueshifted photoionised absorbers moving at approximately $0.1c$ and $0.2c$, the latter being more tentative, or by an alternative collisionally ionised absorption model, which provides a comparably acceptable fit. The presence of ultrafast outflows therefore remains a plausible, but non-unique, interpretation of the data. If associated with outflows, the inferred column densities appear lower than those reported for some persistent ULXs, potentially reflecting differences in the accretion-flow properties or the shorter super-Eddington phase of RX J0209.6-7427.

new.title: Disrupted stars and captured compact objects: Combining observations from multiple messengers to infer the population of massive black holes
new.summary: Massive black holes (MBHs) are found in galactic centres, but their formation and evolution remain elusive. Tidal disruption events (TDEs) and extreme mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) both arise from stellar dynamics in the nuclear star clusters around MBHs, and are observed with electromagnetic surveys and gravitational waves, respectively. To overcome the scarcity of coincident detections, we formulate how to combine gravitational-wave detections from LISA-EMRIs with observations from ZTF-TDEs to measure properties of the MBH population. Building on two-dimensional Fokker-Planck simulations of EMRIs and TDEs, we model how their populations are affected by the MBH-host scaling relation, the nucleation fraction and the MBH occupation fraction, and analyse the resulting catalogues using joint hierarchical inference accounting for their individual selection biases. With current ZTF-TDE detections, we can already identify combinations of MBH formation favoured by and consistent with the observed TDE population, and derive corresponding predictions for the EMRI population detectable by LISA. Across a range of astrophysical assumptions, the ratio of detectable TDEs to EMRIs is high: ZTF detecting 2.7-84.3 times as many TDEs as LISA detects EMRIs. TDEs, through their numbers, set the shared mass and redshift distributions: LSST constrains the characteristic MBH mass to a 90% credible width of 0.31 dex and the power-law index of the redshift evolution to a precision of 0.11. EMRIs make up ~3.4% of the joint catalogue, yet carry more information than the whole ZTF sample and are the only probe of MBH spin and orbital eccentricity. TDEs will constrain the abundance of low-mass MBHs before LISA flies, while EMRIs will measure properties that electromagnetic surveys cannot. EMRI and TDE observations offer complementary insights into MBH growth and evolution that neither can provide alone.

new.title: What determines the properties of Population III binaries?
new.summary: Population~III binaries may provide a gravitational-wave probe of the first stellar populations. Uncertain initial binary parameter distributions and evolutionary prescriptions complicate predictions of their remnant masses, birth orbits and formation spins. Varying these model evolutionary parameters (MEPs) jointly is needed to identify which MEPs shape each property and whether their effects persist among binaries that merge. We use \textsc{StarTrack} to evolve $2\times10^6$ initial binaries per model across 1152 configurations spanning eight MEPs. To our knowledge, this is the largest grid of Population~III isolated-binary population-synthesis models to date by number of distinct parameter configurations. We compare the properties and correlations of all binary black holes (BBHs) with those of systems that merge within the adopted age of the Universe. The all-BBH (merging-BBH) model medians span $34.3$--$171.0 M_{\odot}$ ($23.1$--$94.8 M_{\odot}$) in total mass, $0.039$--$0.106$ ($0.018$--$0.129$) in effective aligned spin $\chi_{\mathrm{eff}}$ at formation, and $0.075$--$0.639$ ($0.039$--$0.983$) in birth eccentricity. Merger selection also changes correlations between BBH properties and the combinations of MEP values and prescriptions associated with them. We use variance-based sensitivity analysis to quantify how the initial binary parameter distributions and evolutionary prescriptions affect the predicted BBH properties.

cross.title: 3D Binary Evolution of a Merging Binary Black Hole Progenitor
cross.summary: Mass transfer is a highly dynamical 3D process that spans evolutionary timescales in binary stars. It is key to the production of gravitational waves through formation of binary black holes and other double compact objects. We integrate global 3D hydrodynamics into stellar evolutionary modeling to resolve mass transfer across nuclear timescales. We employ the shellular approximation in the stellar evolution code MESA to map a 3D spatial structure by equipotential shells in the Roche geometry to maintain hydrostatic equilibrium across tidally-distorted surfaces. We employ the method of time-incremented multiscale evolution to alternate between stellar evolution and 3D hydrodynamics to span large timescales with dynamical feedback. We employ this framework to examine a likely merging binary black hole progenitor system of a low-metallicity 30Msol donor star and 9.3Msol black hole from the end of the main sequence to core Carbon depletion. We modeled two complete mass transfer phases in 3D while self-consistently accounting for stellar evolution. These comprised a thermal-timescale early Case B phase and a nuclear-timescale late Case B phase. The prescription of Kolb & Ritter (1990) closely predicted the results of 3D evolution, except at the end of the first phase of mass transfer; our 3D model remained well-contained by the outer Lagrange point, despite 1D predictions of substantial L3 overflow during this stage. We find incorporating 3D hydrodynamics during Case B mass transfer did not significantly impact expected merger times. Our model never overflowed L3 as predicted by 1D prescriptions. L2/L3 outflows formed even while underflowing those equipotentials. Our model suggests these outflows can be neglected for the evolution of similar systems, but were dense enough to potentially impact X-ray observations.

cross.title: Charge Exchange Illuminates Turbulent Cold-Hot Interfaces
cross.summary: Cold-hot interfaces are ubiquitous in the multiphase circumgalactic medium (CGM), galactic winds, and the Galactic Center (GC), yet their microscopic contact regions are difficult to observe. Charge exchange (CX), in which a highly ionized metal ion captures an electron from a neutral donor and emits soft X-ray lines, directly probes these interfaces. We develop a subgrid CX model coupled to a nonequilibrium ionization (NEI) network in hydrodynamic simulations of radiative turbulent mixing layers. CX soft X-rays are confined to a thin, highly corrugated cold-hot interface (corrugation factor $\sim10$), whereas thermal emission fills the hot phase. Turbulent transport sustains high-charge ions at $T\sim 10^4$-$10^5$ K, where they encounter neutral donors. The low-temperature O VIII fraction exceeds that in a uniformly cooling isobaric parcel, demonstrating the importance of mixing to the ionization history. CX depletes this cool ion population, while continued entrainment maintains the supply. Including a metagalactic ionizing background changes the ion distribution and enhances CX surface brightness by a factor of a few in our CGM comparison, but preserves the cool origin of most CX emission. In the limit of sufficient neutral column, CX surface brightness is ion-supply limited: higher donor density increases local emissivity but shortens the reaction layer. The system-wide CX-to-thermal soft X-ray ratio also depends on the volume-to-interface scale $V/A_{\rm int}$, making CX a potential probe of multiphase structure in the CGM, galactic winds, and the GC.

cross.title: Little Red Dots at Cosmic Noon: Spectroscopy Reveals Declining Abundance but a Non-Evolving Luminosity Function Shape
cross.summary: Little red dots (LRDs) are an extremely abundant population of red, compact, broad-line objects primarily found in the early universe. At $5<z<8$, they are at least 10 times more abundant than UV-selected quasars. Yet, how this population evolves towards lower redshift is unclear. In this work, we present our search for LRDs at cosmic noon ($2\lesssim z\lesssim 4$) in nearly 20 deg$^2$ of the Deep/UltraDeep fields of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). Combining multiwavelength wide-field imaging surveys from 0.3 to 4.5 $\mu$m, we identify 266 photometric LRD candidates. With spectroscopic follow-up from Keck/NIRES, VLT/X-shooter, and Magellan/FIRE on 24 candidates, we identify a sample of four LRDs with broad H$\alpha$ emission. With the purity of the photometric sample calibrated by spectroscopy, we estimate the number density of LRDs to be approximately $6.8\times10^{-7}$ cMpc$^{-3}$ at $2.10<z<2.55$---this is nearly a factor of 35 decrease from their flat number density evolution at $4\lesssim z\lesssim8$ estimated from JWST spectroscopic surveys. The knee of the LRD optical luminosity function also remains consistently at $M_{5500}\approx-22$ mag across $2<z<5$, below that of quasars. We further speculate that only the abundance of LRDs, but not the shape of their optical luminosity function, evolves with redshift, and the Roman Space Telescope will be able to test this decisively with a substantially larger sample of low-redshift LRDs.

cross.title: Accretor Luminosity as Probe of Orbital Evolution and Magnetic Braking in AM CVn Binaries
cross.summary: AM CVn binaries are ultracompact systems with orbital periods $P_{\rm orb} \lesssim 70$ min, where a white dwarf accretes from a He-rich semidegenerate donor. At short orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb} \lesssim 20$ min), rapid accretion reheats the accretor. As the system widens and the mass transfer rate decreases, the accretor follows standard white dwarf cooling at longer orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb} \gtrsim 30$ min). The accretor cooling luminosity then acts as a powerful probe into the orbital evolution of the binary. Recent observations show that the accretor appears brighter (younger) at long orbital periods, compared to models where orbital angular momentum loss is solely set by gravitational wave emission. We show that additional angular momentum loss, which we ascribe to magnetic braking of the donor, can better reproduce observations of accretor luminosity. We test and constrain various proposed magnetic braking formalisms, for the white dwarf, helium star, and evolved cataclysmic variable (CV) channels for AM CVn formation. None of the magnetic braking formalisms in their original form can reproduce the observations, but the widely popular magnetic braking proposed by Rappaport et al. 1983 boosted by a factor $\approx 5$, or the saturated magnetic braking proposed by Matt et al. 2015 boosted by a factor of $\approx 150$, yields satisfactory results. We also find that the CARB formalism, recently applied to the evolved CV channel, is strongly in tension with observations of accretor luminosity. Our models motivate UV spectroscopy observations, and dedicated WD atmosphere models for AM CVn accretors.

cross.title: A Relativistic Newton's Third Law for Binaries in Environments
cross.summary: We derive the relativistic form of Newton's Third Law governing the interaction between intermediate- and extreme-mass-ratio inspirals and surrounding relativistic matter fields. Working within a two-parameter expansion, we rewrite the evolution of the secondary's orbital elements in a form resembling the integrated forces acting on the environment, avoiding the need to calculate any gravitational perturbations sourced by the dynamical matter content. Using the retarded and advanced Green's functions, we obtain both instantaneous and orbit-averaged laws relating the rate of change of the secondary's orbital energy and angular momentum to that of the matter and the gravitational-wave fluxes at that order. Our results clarify and correct the mixture of ad hoc balance prescriptions currently employed in the literature, providing first-principles forcing functions for the secondary's orbital elements in two ready-to-use forms: a leading-order formulation suitable for fast evaluation with complex relativistic matter simulations, and a first-post-adiabatic formulation of the energy and angular-momentum evolution in environments that are stationary and axisymmetric at leading order.

cross.title: Nuclear Urca cooling in magnetar crust and anomalous heating
cross.summary: We present a new result that the nuclear Urca process in magnetars, associated with ultrastrong magnetic field, dramatically alters the neutrino cooling efficiency to support higher surface temper ature, which is not common in ordinary neutron stars. A new formalism for neutrino luminosity accommodating finite temperature on top of magnetic field is extended with the use of realistic nuclear structure inputs for the Urca pair 29Na-29Mg. We find that the neutrino luminosity of Urca pair shows a spiral variation as a function of magnetic field and crust density, while the Urca pair persists, in contrast to previous studies. Applying geometrically correct volumetric energy loss rate to Urca shell at fixed density with varying magnetic field strength, our results show that thermally populated excited states at finite temperature enhance neutrino luminosity, whereas conditions con strained Urca-pair formation driven by ultrastrong magnetic field reduce cooling efficiency, which can explain high temperature of magnetar surface as a new possibility.

cross.title: Nuclear Precision and Multimessenger Constraints on Neutron-Star Structure
cross.summary: Neutron-star cores retain structural freedom beyond the constraints supplied by nuclear measurements. We quantify this freedom through an observable-dependent variance ceiling and identify radius--Love compensation as a mechanism suppressing nuclear constraints on tides. Across four data-conditioned equation-of-state families, a pulsar radius measured to 0.3 km paired with a binary tide measured to 10\% removes 44--68\% of the current logarithmic Love-number variance. The framework connects laboratory precision and complementary stellar measurements to core structure.

repl.title: Jet launching from the Kerr black hole magnetosphere: An electrogeodesic approach
repl.summary: The launch of relativistic jets of plasma on astrophysical to cosmological scales is observed in a variety of astrophysical sources, from active galactic nuclei to X-ray binaries. While these jets can be reproduced by general relativistic magneto-hydrodynamics (GRMHD) and particle-in-cells (GRPIC) simulations of the dynamical Kerr magnetosphere, the development of analytic models to describe the physics of the jets has remained limited. A key challenge is to analytically describe the individual trajectories of accelerated charged particles, which ultimately build up the jet and emit radiation. In this work, we provide a first simple but fully analytical model of jet launching from the Kerr magnetosphere based on the motion of charged particles. To that end, we use the integrability of electrogeodesic motion in the Kerr monopole magnetosphere to study the ejection of charged particles near the poles. This enables us to derive (i) a criterion for the rotation axis to constitute a stable latitudinal equilibrium position, thereby representing an idealized jet, (ii) the expression for the magnetic frame-dragging effect, and (iii) the condition for an asymptotic observer to measure blueshifted particles emanating from the black hole surroundings. Our study reveals that particles can be accelerated only in a specific region whose maximal radius depends on the spin and magnetization of the black hole. We further show that these results extend to the split-monopole Kerr solution by a redefinition of the angular momentum of the charged particles. Alongside these results, we provide a detailed review of the construction of test magnetospheres from (explicit and hidden) symmetries of the Kerr geometry and the condition for the separability of the electrogeodesic motion in a test magnetosphere, which serves as a basis for the model studied in this work.

repl.title: Refined anti-proton and anti-deuteron fluxes from weak-scale Dark Matter
repl.summary: We provide the cosmic-ray (CR) fluxes of antiprotons and antideuterons produced by the Galactic annihilation or decay of weak-scale dark matter (DM) particles of masses in the range from a few GeV to 100 TeV. We estimate these fluxes based on the updated models for the propagation of charged particles in the Galaxy and using the improved $\bar{p}$ and $\bar{d}$ spectra provided by $\texttt{CosmiXs}$. For the updated propagation models we consider the MIN/MED/MAX sets under the new SLIM/BIG/QUAINT schemes. We treat the Galactic propagation in a semi-analytic way including different possible effects such as spatial diffusion, energy-losses, convection and diffusive reacceleration. For the DM distribution in the Galactic halo we consider NFW, Einasto and Burkert profiles with the most updated parameters. Moreover, we also incorporate the latest models for the inelastic cross-sections of $\bar{p}$ and $\bar{d}$ based on ALICE data. We validate our calculations with those available in the literature or those obtained from other publicly available numerical packages. We compare the CR fluxes obtained in this work with those provided previously by $\texttt{PPPC4DMID}$ which were based on old propagation scenarios. We find that the CR fluxes obtained here with the new propagation models are much more robust (compared to the older ones) under the variation MIN - MAX. We also discuss the impact of this in the improvement of the discovery potential of a possible DM signal in the light of the present and upcoming CR observations. We provide all our results for the DM-induced interstellar CR fluxes in a tabulated format (for the kinetic energy range 0.1 GeV - 100 TeV) in the $\texttt{GitHub}$ repository of the newly created $\texttt{CosmiXsPPPC}$ project. The results are ready to be used for studies related to DM indirect searches.

repl.title: Locating the missing baryons in the warm-hot intergalactic medium with fast radio bursts and the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect
repl.summary: Traditional astronomical censuses in the late-time Universe can only account for a fraction of the baryonic matter budget. Hydrodynamical simulations predict that the missing baryons reside in the vast filamentary structures of the cosmic web as a highly diffuse, warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM). Observing the WHIM directly has remained a long-standing challenge due to its typical temperature. In this study, we measure the angular cross-power spectrum between the dispersion measures (DMs) of fast radio bursts (FRBs) from the second CHIME/FRB catalog and the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) Compton-$y$ map from the Planck satellite. After masking cataloged galaxy clusters, we find a positive correlation between FRB DMs and the tSZ map at $>98\%$ confidence ($p_{\rm null}=0.0169$). With a temperature normalization of $2.4\times10^6\ {\rm K}$, we infer that a fraction $f_{\rm WHIM}=0.375^{+0.165}_{-0.161}$ of cosmic baryons resides in the hotter WHIM. These measurements constrain a substantial reservoir of hotter diffuse gas in the cosmic web and statistically close the cosmic baryon budget in the local Universe under the adopted density and pressure model.

repl.title: A systematic search for long GRBs without supernovae: global properties and rate of events
repl.summary: Some long duration gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) are not associated with bright supernovae (SNe), indicating that their explosion mechanism differs from the traditional collapsar channel. SN-less LGRBs are rare, thus it remains unclear whether they are sporadic outliers or a substantial component of the GRB population. In this work, we use two decades of Swift observations to conduct a systematic search for nearby ($z\lesssim$0.35) LGRBs without a confirmed SN association. Our analysis reveals a heterogeneous population linked, in part, to star-forming or dusty environments and, in part, to quiescent galaxies. Through the analysis of their high-energy properties, afterglows, and environments, we identify a sample of LGRBs with robust SN limits and distance scales, more than doubling the number of candidate SN-less events. From our fiducial sample, we derive a volumetric rate, not corrected for beaming, of $R = (0.5 \pm 0.2) {\rm~Gpc^{-3}\ yr^{-1}}$, comparable to the apparent rate of short duration GRBs (SGRBs) and standard LGRBs with SNe with luminosities $L \gtrsim\,10^{50}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$. For plausible beaming factors, the inferred rate of SN-less LGRBs is consistent with several compact binary merger channels, although the allowed parameter space is already narrow if the entire population is attributed to a single progenitor channel. Owing to the small number of candidate events and the uncertainties in their distance scale, our sample leaves the low-luminosity tail unconstrained. A larger sample will be needed to determine whether they are the faint tail of known progenitor channels or evidence of a distinct route to relativistic explosions.

repl.title: Kink instability as a particle acceleration mechanism in X-ray binaries and the connection to the outburst cycle
repl.summary: We consider whether the kink instability can explain particle acceleration in hard state 'compact' X-ray binary jets. We apply a 1D model to assess the expected growth rate of the instability for a variety of jet models, then scale results from simulations to estimate a dissipation rate for the magnetic energy in the jet. We then consider the effects of radiative cooling on the system. We find that hard state 'compact' X-ray binary jets are likely to be unstable to the kink instability within their acceleration zones across a plausible parameter space. We further find that depending on the parameters of the model, the jets may radiate over a variety of length scales ranging from length scales attributable to a 'failed' jet scenario, to those in keeping with resolved radio observations of 'compact' jets. We discuss the expected evolution of this model through the outburst cycle.

repl.title: Widespread steep X-ray spectra of luminous $z=5.85-7.64$ quasars and their implications for future X-ray surveys
repl.summary: Luminous quasars (QSOs) at the Epoch of Reionization (EoR, $z\gtrsim6$) host billion-solar-mass black holes assembled within the first Gyr of cosmic time. Their X-ray emission probes the innermost accreting regions and constrains the physical state of the corona during early supermassive black hole (SMBH) growth. Previous results from the HYPerluminous quasars at the Epoch of ReionizatION (HYPERION) sample of $z \gtrsim 6$ QSOs, powered by the most rapidly accreted SMBHs, suggested a link between X-ray spectral slope and long-term growth efficiency. We test whether the steep X-ray spectra of luminous z>6 QSOs are a general property of early SMBH growth or a peculiarity of the most efficiently grown SMBHs, using a sample extended mainly to the lowest growth efficiencies. We analysed the largest and most X-ray sensitive sample of 28 luminous QSOs at $z = 5.85-7.64$ (26 used in the correlation analysis), combining HYPERION targets, luminous non-HYPERION sources, and QSOs powered by moderately accreting SMBHs newly observed in our XMM-Newton Large Programme. We re-derived black hole masses and growth indicators for the entire sample homogeneously, incorporating the latest JWST-based spectroscopic measurements to ensure the most consistent and high-quality characterization across all targets. We found no statistically significant correlation between coronal spectral parameters and BH growth indicators: luminous $z \gtrsim 6$ QSOs systematically show steep X-ray continua, with high photon indices and/or low high-energy cutoffs, consistent with cold coronae, possibly linked to rapid accretion. Finally, if steep X-ray slopes are common among early AGN, they may significantly reduce count rates, at fixed intrinsic luminosity, in future surveys of the EoR, affecting the detectability of steep-spectrum X-ray sources and thus the census of the early AGN population.

repl.summary: We investigate nuclear pasta phases appearing in hot neutron-star matter based on the compressible liquid-drop model, where the matter consists of a dense liquid phase and a dilute gas phase separated by a sharp this http URL surface tension is calculated self-consistently from the Thomas-Fermi approximation, and it depends on temperature and isospin asymmetry. We employ relativistic mean-field (RMF) models with different symmetry energy slopes to describe nuclear interactions. It is found that the RMF models with smaller symmetry energy slopes result in various pasta phases at low temperatures, whereas those with larger symmetry energy slopes yield only the droplet configuration up to the crust-core transition density. These pasta phases may occur in the inner crust and play an important role in the thermal evolution of the star.

repl.title: Dynamical tidal response of neutron stars: From effective field theory to gravitational waveforms
repl.summary: We investigate the fully relativistic dynamical tidal response of neutron stars up to second order in the frequency. Combining the worldline effective field theory for extended gravitating bodies with perturbation theory of relativistic stellar models, we derive the tidal deformation induced by an external time-dependent field, including a universal logarithmic running term. In the effective theory, we work in dimensional regularization and, through a consistent matching procedure, obtain for the first time the complete leading-order dynamical tidal corrections to both the conservative dynamics and the gravitational-wave signal of compact binaries, including the scheme-dependent finite terms in addition to the running. We show that, in the relativistic regime, dynamical effects cannot be fully captured by mode excitations alone. The magnitude of the additional contribution depends on the stellar compactness, the equation of state, and the running term. Dynamical Love numbers are significantly enhanced with respect to their static counterparts for relatively small compactness. As a result, although they formally enter the gravitational-wave phase at eighth post-Newtonian order, dynamical tidal effects yield a nonnegligible contribution during the late inspiral. Using a Fisher-matrix analysis, we show that third-generation detectors such as the Einstein Telescope could measure dynamical Love numbers for a range of neutron-star masses and equations of state. Conversely, neglecting these effects can lead to significant biases in the inference of static Love numbers, and hence on the nuclear equation of state. Our results highlight the importance of dynamical tidal effects for high-precision gravitational-wave modeling with future detectors.

repl.title: Cataclysmic variables from Gaia XP spectra: The Gaia emission-line magnitude (GEM) diagram
repl.summary: Gaia DR3 opens a new window for the census of Galactic stellar populations in all-sky surveys, specifically for identifying cataclysmic variables (CVs). While the majority of CVs are distributed below the main sequence on the Gaia HR diagram, identifying them among dominant background stellar populations remains a significant challenge. Here, we present the Gaia Emission-line Magnitude (GEM) diagram - a tool designed to isolate CV candidates from background stars located below the main sequence. Using Gaia photometric data and low-resolution BP/RP (XP) spectra, we construct the GEM diagram by plotting the extinction-corrected absolute magnitude ($M_{G0}$) against the pseudo-equivalent width of the H$\alpha$ line ($pgEW_{H\alpha}$), which is computed via a Gaussian line-profile approximation. We find that known CVs and major stellar background populations, including white dwarfs, hot subdwarfs, and white dwarf-main sequence binaries, occupy distinct regions on the GEM diagram, reflecting both their physical properties and the low-resolution nature of the Gaia XP spectra. We define an empirical selection line on the GEM diagram to separate true H$\alpha$-emitting CVs from background contaminants. As a proof of concept, we apply the GEM diagram to a Gaia volume-limited sample within 250 pc ($G<17.5$ mag) distributed below the main sequence, recovering known CVs. Additionally, we identify three new CV candidates whose accreting nature is supported by archival X-ray data and optical variability. Compared to traditional optical color-based selection techniques, the GEM diagram uses Gaia's low-resolution spectra for initial target identification in all-sky surveys. This provides a more reliable framework for the statistical selection of CV candidates prior to ground-based spectroscopic follow-up and can be scaled to future Gaia data releases to map Galactic emission-line star populations.

From top to bottom, panels display: CVs; WDs; WD+MS binaries; and hot subdwarfs. The position of H α \alpha is indicated by a vertical dashed line. Only objects where the H α \alpha line was identified were used to compute the median spectra. A prominent H α \alpha emission line is visible for CVs, whereas absorption lines are present in the WDs and hot subdwarfs. The H α \alpha emission feature in WD+MS binaries likely results from chromospheric emission, pseudo-emission artifacts of TiO molecular bands from the M-dwarf companion in the low-resolution Gaia XP spectra, or a combination of both.
